title: Accent marks
goal: By the end of this lesson you can name the five French accent marks, pronounce é, è and ê correctly, use accents that change meaning (à / a, où / ou), and hear the Quebec difference between pâte and patte.

body: French accents are not decoration: they are part of the spelling, and a missing accent is a spelling mistake. Some change the sound, some only change the meaning.
The five marks are the *accent aigu* (é), the *accent grave* (è, à, ù), the *accent circonflexe* (â, ê, î, ô, û), the *cédille* (ç) and the *tréma* (ë, ï, ü).

learn.h: é, è, ê: three ways to write two sounds
body: *é* (accent aigu) is a closed sound, like 'ay' in 'say' but short and without gliding: *café*, *été*, *bébé*. The ending *-er* of verbs and *-ez* also make this sound: *parler*, *vous parlez*.
*è* and *ê* are open sounds, like 'e' in 'bed': *mère*, *très*, *fête*, *forêt*. A plain *e* with no accent is usually 'uh' (*le*, *petit*) or silent at the end of a word (*table*).
learn.tip: The accent aigu 'points up' to a closed, tight sound; the grave 'points down' to an open one.

body: On *a* and *u*, the accent grave does not change the sound. It tells you which word it is: *a* (has) vs *à* (to, at), *ou* (or) vs *où* (where), *la* (the) vs *là* (there).

The circumflex can also separate words: *sur* (on) vs *sûr* (sure), *du* (some) vs *dû* (owed). It often replaces an old s that English still has: *forêt* (forest), *hôpital* (hospital), *fête* (feast).
learn.tip: Circumflex + English s: forêt/forest, île/isle, hôtel/hostel, pâte/paste.

body: Before *a, o, u*, a plain *c* is hard (k): *café*, *comment*. The cédille makes it soft (s): *ça*, *garçon*, *reçu*. You never need it before *e* or *i*, where c is already soft (*merci*, *ici*).
The tréma tells you to pronounce two vowels separately: *naïf* is na-eef, not 'nef'; *Noël* is no-el. *maïs* (corn) is ma-eess, while *mais* (but) is 'meh'.

learn.h: Quebec: â and ê stay long
body: In France today, *pâte* (dough, paste) and *patte* (paw) usually sound the same. In Quebec they are clearly different: *pâte* has a long, deep 'aw' sound [pawt], *patte* a short, bright 'a' [pat].
The same goes for *ê*: *fête* (party) is long and can glide to 'faète', while *faite* (done, feminine) is short. Quebecers really use this length to tell words apart, so listen for it.

examples.note: è in mère and très = open 'eh'
two é's in été; Québec has é
à = in/at; without the accent, a means 'has'
où = where; hôtel has a circumflex (old s: hostel)
Quebec: long, deep â in pâte

examples.fr: Le chien a mal à la patte.
examples.en: The dog has a sore paw.
examples.note: short a in patte; a = has, à = at

quebec.intro: Quebec French keeps long vowels that France has mostly lost. A circumflex often marks a long vowel: pâte sounds like 'pawt', clearly different from patte.

items.std: la pâte / la patte (same sound in Paris)
items.note: the circumflex â is long and deep in Quebec
same long, deep â; pronunciation only
informal: a before a final r is also long and deep in Quebec
informal: long ê glides, c'est une → c't'une
long ê/î: not the same as mettre

drills.q: Which accent can ONLY go on the letter e?
drills.why: The accent aigu appears only on é.

options: To make the c sound like s before o
To make the c sound like k
drills.why: Before a, o, u, c is hard unless it has a cédille.

drills.q: In Quebec, which pair sounds clearly different?
drills.why: Quebec keeps the long â of pâte. The other pairs sound identical everywhere.
sûr needs the circumflex; add -e for a woman.

vocab.ex: Le chat a mal à la patte.

pron.tip: Tréma: two separate vowels. no-EL, na-EEF.

dialogue.fr: Bonjour! Un café ou un thé?
dialogue.en: Hello! A coffee or a tea?

dialogue.fr: Oui, merci. Où sont les toilettes?
dialogue.en: Yes, thank you. Where are the washrooms?

dialogue.fr: Merci. Et la pâte à pizza, elle est prête?
dialogue.en: Thanks. And the pizza dough, is it ready?

questions.q: What does B ask about at the end?

speak.prompt: Read aloud and make the é / è contrast clear: 'Mon père a été très gentil.'
speak.model: mõ PÈR a ay-TAY trè zhahn-TEE

speak.prompt: Say both words with the Quebec contrast: pâte, patte.
Ask where three places are, using où.
speak.model: Où est l'hôtel? Où est le café? Où est la forêt?

write.prompt: Copy these words and add the missing accents: cafe, ete, tres, ou (where), ca, garcon, Noel, hotel. Then write two short sentences with them.
write.model: café, été, très, où, ça, garçon, Noël, hôtel. Où est l'hôtel? Le garçon est très gentil.

quiz.q: The circumflex in 'forêt' often replaces which old letter?

quiz.why: français: c before a needs ç to sound like s.

quiz.q: What does the tréma in 'maïs' tell you?
Which accent mark does NOT change the sound of a or u?
quiz.why: à and ù sound like a and u; the accent only changes the meaning.
Quebec keeps long â distinct from short a.

quiz.q: Which word is pronounced with an open 'eh' sound?
quiz.why: è in très is open; é, -er are closed.

quiz.q: Is a missing accent a spelling mistake in French?
quiz.why: Accents are part of the spelling, including on capitals (the OQLF recommends them).
